weeks.title: Python core
weeks.focus_hours: Mon 1 Jun · 10 hours total · translation not learning
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: Python has no types by default (add them with hints). No semicolons. Indentation IS the block. def = void/method. self = this. dict = Dictionary. list = List. That's 80% of the translation work.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday night you can write a Python class, call a function with typed parameters, read/write a JSON file, and run a script from the terminal. Nothing more.

tasks.content: Install Python 3.12 + VS Code + Python extension (15 min)
Watch Corey Schafer: Python Tutorial for Beginners #1 and #2 — variables, strings, numbers (30 min)
Open a .py file and replicate every example as you watch (15 min)
Watch Corey Schafer #3: Lists, Tuples — note how they differ from List<T> (20 min)
Write a function that takes a patient name + age and prints a formatted summary C# → Python
Add type hints: def greet(name: str, age: int) -> str
Watch Corey Schafer #4: Dicts — your replacement for Dictionary<string,object> (20 min)
Build a Patient dict: {"name": "Ali", "age": 34, "insurance": "NHIF"}
Write a function that reads a list of patient dicts and filters by insurance type
Watch Corey Schafer #5 + #6: Functions + conditionals (30 min)
Note: elif not else if. is None not == null. Write 5 examples (20 min)
Read: Python type hints cheat sheet — bookmark it (10 min)
Watch Corey Schafer #7: Classes + OOP (20 min)
Convert your patient dict into a Patient class with __init__, a method get_summary()
self = this, __init__ = constructor. Write it. Run it.
Setup: create a virtual env python -m venv .venv, activate it, install nothing yet (20 min)
Build patient_registry.py — a PatientRegistry class that holds a list of Patient objects, can add/find/list them (60 min)
Read/write to a JSON file: json.dump() to save, json.load() to restore (40 min)
Run it from terminal. Fix all errors. (60 min)
Read back your code from the week — add docstrings to every function ("""Does X""")
Compare: write the same Patient class in C# side by side. See the 1:1 mapping.
Push to a new GitHub repo called genai-journey. This is where all 6 months live.

weeks.title: Async + FastAPI
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · Poetry, pip, async/await, virtual environments, FastAPI basics
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: async/await works the same conceptually but Python has a single event loop (like Node.js) not threads. pip = NuGet CLI. Poetry = your .csproj + NuGet combined. FastAPI = ASP.NET Minimal API but in 10 lines.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you have a running FastAPI server with 2 endpoints. You understand async/await in Python vs C#. You manage packages with Poetry. You never use the system Python again.

tasks.content: Install Poetry: pip install poetry. Create a new project: poetry new ai-clinical (15 min)
Read: what's the difference between pip, venv, conda, and Poetry — one page, then forget the others (15 min)
Watch Corey Schafer: Modules and Pip (#9) — understand how imports work (30 min)
Watch Corey Schafer: Decorators (#16) — FastAPI uses decorators for everything, you need this (30 min)
Write 5 examples using decorators: @property, custom decorator that logs function calls
Understand: @app.get("/patients") is just a decorator registering a route handler
Watch: Python async/await explained (TechWithTim or ArjanCodes) (30 min)
Write: an async function that pretends to fetch patient data (await asyncio.sleep(1))
Note: asyncio.run(main()) = app.Run(). Same pattern.
FastAPI official docs: First Steps — read and run hello world (20 min)
FastAPI: Path Parameters + Query Parameters — same as ASP.NET route params (20 min)
FastAPI: Pydantic models — this is your record / DTO class. (20 min)
Build your first FastAPI app: main.py with a GET /health and POST /patient endpoint (30 min)
Define a PatientRequest Pydantic model with name, age, insurance fields
Run with uvicorn main:app --reload and open auto Swagger at /docs
Extend your FastAPI app: add POST /analyze-symptoms endpoint — accepts a list of symptoms, returns a mock response for now (60 min)
Add error handling: HTTPException, what happens when input is invalid (30 min)
Add environment variables: create a .env file, load with python-dotenv (30 min)
Test all endpoints from Swagger UI. Write a simple test_main.py with pytest (60 min)
Draw request lifecycle diagram. Same as your Blazor middleware mental model.
Update your README.md in genai-journey: what you built, how to run it
Push everything. Week 3 starting point is this FastAPI project.

weeks.title: OpenAI + Claude APIs
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · chat completions, streaming, system prompts, calling from Python AND C#
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: The OpenAI API is just an HTTP POST to /v1/chat/completions. You can call it with HttpClient in C# — no special SDK needed. The Python SDK is just a wrapper. Streaming = server-sent events, same as your existing Blazor streaming patterns.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you have a working FastAPI endpoint that calls an LLM and streams the response back. You've called the same API from C# too. Your AI Clinical Assistant is running end-to-end.

tasks.content: Get your API key: platform.openai.com — add $5 credit. Store in .env. (10 min)
Read the OpenAI Chat Completions quickstart — understand: messages array, role: system/user/assistant, model, temperature (30 min)
Run the 10-line Python example from their docs. See a response. You're now an AI developer. (20 min)
Write a llm_service.py module with one function: async def ask(system: str, user: str) -> str
Call it with a medical system prompt: "You are a clinical assistant. Be concise and factual."
Print the response. Change temperature from 0 to 1 — see what changes.
Add streaming: use stream=True, iterate the chunks, print each token as it arrives
Get a Claude API key: console.anthropic.com — free tier available (10 min)
Call Claude with the same prompt using the anthropic Python package. Compare the responses.
Read: OpenAI token pricing page. Understand: prompt tokens + completion tokens = cost. (20 min)
Read: the difference between gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, claude-sonnet (20 min)
NOW call the API from C#: use HttpClient to POST to OpenAI directly, no SDK. Parse the JSON response. (20 min)
Wire your llm_service.py into your FastAPI POST /analyze-symptoms endpoint from Week 2
Build the system prompt: tell the LLM it's a clinical assistant, give it the symptoms, ask for possible conditions
Test it from Swagger UI with real symptom inputs.
Complete the AI Clinical Assistant: clean up the FastAPI app, add proper error handling for API failures (60 min)
Add a second endpoint: POST /insurance-check — takes patient + insurance type, returns coverage summary (60 min)
Add the ICD-10 suggester to your AKHSmart Blazor app — a button in ClaimDetails that calls Claude API from C# (60 min)
Write down: what is a system prompt, why does it matter in your own words
Push: AI Clinical Assistant folder to genai-journey repo with a README
Push: the ICD-10 suggester commit to AKHSmart

weeks.title: Prompt engineering & structured outputs
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · function calling, JSON mode, prompt patterns, Insurance Authorization project
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: Function calling = you define a method signature (in JSON schema), the LLM decides when to "call" it and fills in the parameters. It never actually calls your function — it just returns a structured JSON saying "I want to call X with these args." You then call your real function. Think of it as the LLM filling out a typed form.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can make an LLM return reliable, structured JSON that you can map to a C# or Python object. You know 5 prompt patterns by name and when to use each. Your Insurance Authorization Assistant is done.

tasks.content: Read: OpenAI Structured Outputs docs — response_format: { type: "json_schema" } (20 min)
Run the example: ask GPT to return a JSON object with specific fields. See how it never deviates. (20 min)
Read: Anthropic prompt engineering guide — focus on the "be specific" and "use XML tags" sections (20 min)
Write a prompt that returns a structured authorization checklist in JSON: {"approved": bool, "reasons": [], "missing_documents": []}
Parse the JSON response into a Pydantic model: class AuthorizationResult(BaseModel)
If the parse fails — add a retry. This is real-world LLM reliability work.
Learn function calling: define a check_insurance_eligibility tool schema with patient_id and insurance_type params
When the LLM returns a tool_call, handle it: call your fake check_eligibility() function, return result to LLM
This is the foundation of agents. Understand the loop: LLM → tool call → your code → LLM again
Learn 5 prompt patterns — write one example of each (45 min):
Zero-shot, Few-shot, Chain-of-thought, System persona, and XML tags
Test: which pattern gives the most reliable output for clinical data? (15 min)
Start the Insurance Authorization Assistant: new FastAPI endpoint POST /authorization
Input model: patient name, diagnosis code, procedure, insurance type
Write system prompt using XML tags pattern + few-shot examples. Return structured JSON.
Complete Insurance Authorization Assistant — full endpoint, Pydantic model for output, proper error handling (90 min)
Test with 5 different inputs: NHIF, Jubilee, Staff insurance — tune the prompt. (45 min)
Improve ICD-10 suggester in AKHSmart: use structured output to return exactly 3 codes with confidence scores as JSON, not plain text (45 min)
Month 1 retrospective: write 5 things you learned, 2 things that confused you, 1 thing you want to go deeper on
Push both projects with clean READMEs: AI Clinical Assistant + Insurance Authorization Assistant
You are now ready for Month 2 (LangChain). The foundation is solid.

weeks.title: LangChain Essentials & Chains
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · LCEL chains, prompt templates, output parsers, memory
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: LangChain's RunnableSequence (using | pipe) is simply a functional Pipe-and-Filter or Middleware pipeline. Prompt templates are just advanced string interpolators. Output parsers replace manual JSON deserialization loops.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can build a functional sequence using LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) that feeds structured prompts into Claude/OpenAI and parses the output back into typed Python objects.

tasks.content: Install LangChain core: pip install langchain langchain-openai langchain-community (15 min)
Read LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) concepts — focus on runnable components (30 min)
Setup LangSmith API key in your .env. This is your essential visual debugger! (15 min)
Practice PromptTemplates: write templates with multiple variables (e.g. patient name, diagnostic report) (20 min)
Learn Output Parsers: use PydanticOutputParser to define an expected medical schema (30 min)
Write a function that hooks Prompt -> Model -> Output Parser together using standard python code. (10 min)
Rebuild Tuesday's workflow using LCEL pipe notation: chain = prompt | model | parser (20 min)
Run the chain asynchronously with await chain.ainvoke({"input": "..."}) (20 min)
Open LangSmith dashboard to trace the payload execution graph step-by-step. (20 min)
Understand memory: check ConversationBufferMemory vs ConversationBufferWindowMemory (30 min)
Implement SQLite persistent history: store conversation logs to a local db using SQLChatMessageHistory (30 min)
Build a Claim Appeal Generator chain: feeds claim denial notes and returns a polite medical appeal letter (30 min)
Add conversation history: verify it references the original claim denial during follow-up messages (30 min)
Setup: Create a FastAPI app in a new folder policy-qa. Configure poetry dependency settings. (30 min)
Implement policy chat route: receives user questions and queries policies (use mock text for policies today) (60 min)
Add chat memory so doctors can ask follow-ups. Stream token responses via StreamingResponse (60 min)
Trace all calls in LangSmith to verify latency optimization. (30 min)
Review your LangSmith trace dashboard. Understand token usage and performance bottle necks. (60 min)
Read: LangChain security guidelines (data leakage, prompt injections) (30 min)
Push week 5 code to your repository. (30 min)

weeks.title: Document Workflows & Retrieval Chains
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · Document loaders, text splitting, custom tools, retrieval chains
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: Document loaders replace StreamReader file parser scripts. Splitting text is equivalent to chunking data for memory-efficient indexing. Custom tools map to delegate callbacks or reflection-based class bindings.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can load a PDF policy manual, split it into chunks with optimized overlaps, and register custom Python functions as tools for models to invoke.

tasks.content: Understand loaders: check PyPDFLoader, Docx2txtLoader, and TextLoader (30 min)
Install dependencies: pip install pypdf docx2txt and load a clinical PDF document (30 min)
Practice splitting: compare CharacterTextSplitter vs RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter (30 min)
Print output chunks: notice how headers are retained. Test different chunk sizes (e.g. 500 tokens, 1000 tokens) (30 min)
Define a custom python function that calculates medical pricing formulas. (20 min)
Register the function as a model tool using the @tool decorator, adding clear docstrings. (20 min)
Bind tools to the chat model: model.bind_tools([my_tool]) (20 min)
Read tool dispatch flows: how models output structured tool calls and how to invoke the matching python function automatically. (30 min)
Review parallel tool calling patterns in LangChain. (30 min)
Add error handling to tool execution: capture exceptions and send them back to the LLM as observation context. (40 min)
Setup tool retries if validation fails. (20 min)
Start the Hospital Policy Assistant: configure document loaders to read the clinical PDF files (45 min)
Build ingestion workflow: load files, extract headers, split recursively, attach metadata (source file, category) (75 min)
Connect to FastAPI: write a route POST /ingest that processes uploaded files. (60 min)
Inspect metadata output logs. Verify text formatting in split blocks is clean. (60 min)
Push Hospital Policy Assistant (Part 1) to GitHub. (60 min)

weeks.title: LangGraph Agent Workflows (State & Nodes)
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · StateGraph, nodes, edges, conditional routing, cyclic graphs
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: LangGraph is a State Machine engine (like Windows Workflow Foundation or stateless state machines). Nodes represent action methods. Edges determine branching rules. State is the shared context thread.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can build a cyclic state graph where nodes execute API tasks, modify a shared workflow state dictionary, and dynamically branch based on model choices.

tasks.content: Install LangGraph: pip install langgraph (15 min)
Read LangGraph concepts: StateGraph, Nodes, Edges, entry points. (45 min)
Define a custom TypedDict representing your application state variables. (20 min)
Write 2 nodes: one that reads input, one that formats and writes output variables. (20 min)
Assemble the graph, compile it, and invoke with input values. (20 min)
Learn Conditional Edges: write routing functions that examine state values and direct execution paths. (30 min)
Build a simple branching graph (e.g. if input contains 'urgent' route to high-priority node). (30 min)
Understand cyclic graphs: write loops where execution goes back to an earlier node if validation metrics fail. (45 min)
Study agent design pattern: LLM node -> Tool Call node -> Observation node -> loop back. (15 min)
Implement cyclic validation loops: create a state graph where the LLM corrects structured output schema if validation fails. (60 min)
Start the Smart Claims Validation Pipeline: create the State schema (includes claim inputs, errors list, verification status) (45 min)
Write pipeline nodes: Node 1 checks Oracle DB (mock) for membership info. Node 2 checks pre-auth coverage. Node 3 evaluates billing consistency. (75 min)
Assemble and test: compile graph workflows. Verify errors are collected in state history. (60 min)
Examine the compiled graph structure visually using graphviz / ASCII exports. (40 min)
Ensure state accumulation works. Push pipeline layout to Git. (80 min)

weeks.title: Human-in-the-Loop & Checked Workflows
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · State checkpointers, breakpoints, manual approval gates, custom modifications
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: Breakpoints are asynchronous workflow savepoints. Pausing/resuming state graphs mirrors database persistence of long-running workflows with manual gateway reviews.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can pause agent executions before executing sensitive actions, persist intermediate state databases, and resume workflows after manual user approvals.

tasks.content: Read checkpointer concepts in LangGraph: understand how state is persisted at each step. (30 min)
Setup a simple memory database checkpointer: MemorySaver (30 min)
Implement breakpoints: compile your state graph specifying interrupt_before sensitive nodes. (30 min)
Run the graph: verify execution halts and waits at the specified breakpoint step. (30 min)
Resume paused workflows: pass human approval input back to the checkpointer state and call `resume` to finish. (40 min)
Verify state updates are preserved. (20 min)
Understand state editing: how humans can correct values directly inside intermediate state databases before resuming execution. (45 min)
Study SqliteSaver configs. (15 min)
Write automated unit tests for state graphs, mocking external services. (60 min)
Complete Smart Claims Validation Pipeline: add checkpointer database persistence using SqliteSaver (60 min)
Add manual audit: pause claims exceeding $5,000, requiring manual approval inputs before finalizing db records (90 min)
Expose API routes in FastAPI to inspect paused states and post approval decisions. (30 min)
Complete Month 2 Retrospective. Review the pipeline flow. (40 min)
Deploy pipeline details, screenshots, and logs to Git. (80 min)

weeks.title: Embeddings & Vector Stores (ChromaDB)
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · Vector embeddings, similarity searches, ChromaDB integration
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: A vector database is similar to Lucene.NET or SQL indexes, but optimized for high-dimensional float array cosine similarity checks. It finds matching concepts rather than keyword patterns.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you understand how text is transformed into float vector arrays, can write queries to check cosine similarity, and build collections in a local ChromaDB instance.

tasks.content: Study vector embedding concepts: dimensions, cosine similarity, distance metrics. (40 min)
Generate sample embeddings using OpenAI's API: text-embedding-3-small (20 min)
Install ChromaDB: pip install chromadb (15 min)
Initialize a persistent client. Create a collection called policies. (20 min)
Add 5 sample document strings with IDs and query closest results. (25 min)
Practice query distance parameters. Compare Cosine Similarity, L2 Euclidean Distance, and Inner Product. (30 min)
Inspect query response metadata. (30 min)
Learn Metadata Filtering: write queries filtering vectors by dictionary properties (e.g. {"insurer": "NHIF"}). (40 min)
Understand where filters fit in indexing. (20 min)
Write a C# helper console app to request embeddings via HTTP and compare semantic sorting output results to Python. (60 min)
Start the Local Policy Query Tool: read policy FAQs from a local JSON document. (45 min)
Ingest QA pairs into ChromaDB, creating auto-embeddings via client configs. (75 min)
Write CLI: receives search phrases, runs query with filter options, outputs closest answer. (60 min)
Test CLI results using semantic rephrases. Check if matching answers return. (60 min)
Push code to Git. (60 min)

weeks.title: Enterprise Vector Search (Qdrant)
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · Qdrant client, payloads, schema indices, Docker setup, text chunking
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: ChromaDB is SQLite; Qdrant is SQL Server / Postgres. A scalable cluster instance running via Docker containers. High performance, transaction safety, and schema validation index layers.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can launch Qdrant using Docker containers, configure payload schema indexing filters, and load processed document chunks into enterprise storage pools.

tasks.content: Launch Qdrant via Docker: docker run -p 6333:6333 qdrant/qdrant (30 min)
Read Qdrant vector database concepts: points, payloads, indexes. (30 min)
Install Qdrant python client: pip install qdrant-client (15 min)
Connect to Docker instance. Create a collection defining vector size and distance configuration. (45 min)
Practice upserting: define payload attributes (id, vector, metadata dictionaries). (30 min)
Understand points updates: how to modify payloads without rewriting vector records. (30 min)
Learn advanced payload filtering: range criteria, nested conditions, exact match blocks. (40 min)
Study index speed tuning. (20 min)
Practice document chunking layout: write a script to calculate overlaps when text chunks contain tables or lists. (60 min)
Start AKHST Knowledge Assistant: index medical policy PDFs (NHIF, Jubilee, ZHSF) (60 min)
Build ingestion logic: parse, recursively split, generate vectors, upload to Qdrant with detailed metadata payloads. (90 min)
Verify collection points count in Qdrant dashboard at http://localhost:6333/dashboard (30 min)
Test search responses. Validate metadata properties map correctly. (60 min)
Push code to Git. (60 min)

weeks.title: Production Retrieval (Hybrid Search & Re-ranking)
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · Hybrid search (dense + sparse), BM25, Cohere re-ranking, FlashRank
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: Hybrid search matches combining Full-Text Indexing (LIKE queries) with vector matching scores. Re-ranking is similar to sorting list items using complex secondary scoring filters.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can combine semantic vectors with traditional BM25 text queries in a single query pipeline and apply re-ranking model layers to retrieve the top 3 high-relevance chunks.

tasks.content: Read Hybrid Search concepts: Sparse Vectors (BM25 lexical) vs Dense Vectors (Semantic embeddings). (45 min)
Compare pros and cons of each method. (15 min)
Setup sparse indices in Qdrant collections. (30 min)
Run query combining semantic score and text relevance metrics. (30 min)
Learn Re-ranking: setup cohere-client or lightweight local flashrank (30 min)
Ingest 10 retrieved vectors, re-rank, and select the top 3 with highest scores. (30 min)
Read NirDiamant/RAG_Techniques patterns: focus on context compression and token management. (45 min)
Compare chunk sorting styles. (15 min)
Build context compression utility: summarizes raw retrieved text blocks to match Claude's context limits. (60 min)
Develop AKHST Knowledge Assistant (Part 2): create a retrieval query script. (45 min)
Implement Hybrid Search (Dense + BM25) and filter by insurer metadata. (75 min)
Add Re-ranking using Cohere API to get the top 3 chunks, and feed them into Claude. (60 min)
Compare search precision using semantic search alone vs hybrid search + re-ranking. (60 min)
Push updates to Git. (60 min)

weeks.title: Context Enrichment & Parent-Child Retrieval
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · Parent-document retriever, sentence window retrieval, hierarchical chunking
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: Parent-Child mapping is similar to database relationships (One-to-Many). Search query targets children keys, but loads primary tables when formatting output contexts.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can set up a parent-child indexing schema where search queries match small text chunks but retrieve the broader parent context parameters.

tasks.content: Read Parent-Document Retrieval concepts: index small, descriptive sub-chunks for similarity matches, link to parent document IDs. (45 min)
Compare to plain chunking. (15 min)
Setup ingestion flow: split documents into parents (e.g. 2000 chars) and child nodes (e.g. 400 chars). (40 min)
Store child vectors containing parent IDs. (20 min)
Write retrieval step: query closest child vectors, retrieve parent document text using the linked parent IDs. (60 min)
Understand Sentence Window Retrieval: match a target sentence, but retrieve surrounding sentence windows (e.g. +/- 2 sentences). (40 min)
Review NirDiamant RAG patterns. (20 min)
Implement Sentence Window helper in Python: processes splits and resolves surrounding indices dynamically. (60 min)
Develop Context Enrichment Pipeline: load policy manuals, ingest using sentence window metadata formatting. (90 min)
Expose API endpoints to test querying using child matches and parent context expansion. (60 min)
Verify prompt accuracy inside LangSmith dashboard. (30 min)
Review sentence mapping structures. Push context enrichment codes to Git. (65 min)
Verify index storage sizes. (55 min)

weeks.title: RAG Evaluation & Safety Guardrails
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · RAGAS framework, hallucination filters, LLM-as-judge, input validation
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: Evaluation is similar to unit testing, but for semantic verification. Asserting faithfulness replaces static assertions, verifying output consistency over test cases.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can run RAGAS benchmark metrics to score answer quality, create LLM-as-judge prompts to detect clinical hallucinations, and build input validation filters.

tasks.content: Understand RAG Evaluation: learn Faithfulness (factuality) vs Answer Relevance vs Context Precision. (45 min)
Install RAGAS: pip install ragas (15 min)
Setup RAGAS metrics. Compile a test dataset containing query, context, and output response. (40 min)
Run evaluation and print the scores dashboard. (20 min)
Write an LLM-as-judge validator prompt: tells a secondary model to audit output facts against context references. (35 min)
Validate clinical correctness. (25 min)
Learn input safety guardrails: prevent prompt injections and filter out HIPAA-sensitive PII before requests reach models. (45 min)
Study LLM Guard libraries. (15 min)
Write validation wrapper: intercepts responses and checks them against safety rules before returning. (60 min)
Complete AKHST Knowledge Assistant: assemble full retrieval server (60 min)
Integrate validation layers: check for hallucinations, verify citations exist, filter inputs. (60 min)
Create automated benchmarks script: runs RAGAS on 20 policy scenarios, outputting a performance report. (60 min)
Month 3 retrospective: verify RAG accuracy scores. (45 min)
Push all codes and report documents to Git. (75 min)

weeks.title: Agent Architectures & ReAct Loops
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · ReAct loop, tool registry, dynamic dispatch, stop conditions
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: A ReAct loop is an asynchronous while(true) loop containing a state transition switch block. The LLM's thought outputs determine the next case statement.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can write a custom reasoning-and-acting execution loop from scratch without high-level libraries, handling tool extraction and loop stops.

tasks.content: Read ReAct agent pattern: understand Thought -> Action -> Observation cycle. (45 min)
Compare to plain prompting styles. (15 min)
Write parser script: inspect LLM completions for specific keywords (e.g. `Action: search_policy[arg]`). (30 min)
Test regex patterns. (30 min)
Build execution step: execute python functions based on parsed action names, and pass return values back to prompt history. (60 min)
Understand loop stop criteria: define maximum cycles limits, check token limits, and handle infinite execution loop blocks. (40 min)
Review NirDiamant agent codes. (20 min)
Implement execution limits: write a handler checking runtime parameters, stopping loops if exceptions occur. (60 min)
Develop Invoice Auditor Agent: register tools for membership queries, billing checks, and math formulas. (60 min)
Write raw loop running loops: agent searches invoices, calls tools, and writes formatted audit summaries. (90 min)
Test run tracing in LangSmith dashboard. (30 min)
Identify loop bottlenecks in your code. Push custom ReAct loop codes to Git. (60 min)
Verify error recovery parameters. (60 min)

weeks.title: Multi-Agent Systems with CrewAI
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · CrewAI core, specialized roles, collaborative tasks, context sharing
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: CrewAI maps to Orchestrator or Saga workflows. A sequence of service workers, each carrying unique configurations, modifying shared context data files.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can build a collaborative multi-agent group using CrewAI, assign sequential tasks, and share context files between specialist workers.

tasks.content: Read CrewAI framework core: understand Agent configs, Task definitions, and Crew orchestration parameters. (45 min)
Install CrewAI: pip install crewai (15 min)
Define specialized agents: create configs specifying distinct backstories, target goals, and role descriptors. (35 min)
Run simple group loops. (25 min)
Configure agent handoffs: create sequential tasks where agent 2 reads output files produced by agent 1. (60 min)
Read: Microsoft's AI Agents for Beginners course: focus on collaboration models and memory buffers. (45 min)
Review AutoGen structures. (15 min)
Setup agent tools delegation: controls whether agents can share tasks or delegate execution targets dynamically. (60 min)
Develop Insurance Multi-Agent System (Part 1): setup Crew configs (45 min)
Create 2 agents: (1) Claims Analyst (audits codes, compares rules), (2) Auditor Agent (flags suspicious billings, formats summaries). (75 min)
Orchestrate crew workflows, sending mock claim data files. Run execution. (60 min)
Review intermediate agent chat histories. Push CrewAI codes to Git. (60 min)
Check validation parameters. (60 min)

weeks.title: C# Semantic Kernel Agents (Parallel Practice)
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · Semantic Kernel (.NET 10), native plugins, ChatHistory loops, C# database queries
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: Fully integrated in the Microsoft .NET 10 ecosystem. Dependency injection (IServiceCollection), C# methods as plugins, and typed models. LangChain tools map to C# class methods.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can create native LLM plugins in C# using Semantic Kernel, register database queries as functions, and run typed agent loops inside Blazor projects.

tasks.content: Setup Semantic Kernel packages in a .NET 10 project: Microsoft.SemanticKernel (30 min)
Read Semantic Kernel design patterns: kernel builders, plugins, connector systems. (30 min)
Write Native C# Plugins: map class methods using [KernelFunction] and describe parameters with [Description]. (40 min)
Verify parameter registration. (20 min)
Build chat execution loops: use ChatHistory, append roles context, and fetch completions via IChatCompletionService. (60 min)
Understand multi-agent coordination in C#: learn ChatCompletionAgent and AgentGroupChat configurations. (45 min)
Study C# agent templates. (15 min)
Setup database connections: write native C# plugins that connect to mock database files and run queries. (60 min)
Build Claims Processing Agent (C# version): create console client and integrate Semantic Kernel core. (60 min)
Register native SQL query plugins connecting to simulated databases. (60 min)
Configure LLM tool calling loops: agent queries table, parses claims details, asks model to check rules, outputs audit records. (60 min)
Review C# dependency mappings. Push Semantic Kernel codes to Git repository. (60 min)
Verify JSON parsing speeds. (60 min)

weeks.title: Production Agent Workflows
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · Hierarchical routers, LangGraph supervisor, state merges, safety guardrails
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: Hierarchical routing mirrors centralized workflow controllers delegating sub-tasks to microservices, compiling outputs before returning response payloads.

weeks.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Architecture
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours total · Model Context Protocol, stdio transport, Claude Desktop, JSON-RPC 2.0
weeks.csharp_mindset: C# dev mindset: MCP is gRPC or OpenAPI but optimized specifically for LLMs. A standardized JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol over stdio streams or Server-Sent Events (SSE).
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you understand the MCP JSON-RPC spec, can build an stdio MCP server in Python, and configure Claude Desktop to query it for local tool outputs.

tasks.content: Read Model Context Protocol specification: understand Client, Host, and Server roles. (45 min)
Review transport mechanics. (15 min)
Install MCP python SDK: pip install mcp (15 min)

Configure Claude Desktop: add your python server entry point to claude_desktop_config.json file. (30 min)
Launch Claude Desktop: verify tool shows up in prompt inputs. (30 min)
Study MCP C# SDK: check how stdio streams and tool schemas are configured in .NET projects. (40 min)
Review JSON-RPC 2.0 specifications. (20 min)
